- [ ] **T-045** Verify the vault-isolation leak stays closed — **FIXED and SHIPPED as v0.22.1 (`e633fcb`, diagnosed by Atlas, committed by Forge, Session 53). The guard caught its own committer on day one.** The test suite had been writing session summaries into Aaron's **real** Obsidian vault: 13 files named `2026-08-31-ob-server-{slug}.md`, 69 bytes each, frontmatter `project: ob-server-Cz4UxZ` with an empty `sessionId` and a body of `test`. Found at `/end` while listing `Summaries/`. **This is a recurrence with the guard already in place** — `tests/setup-env.ts` has set `OPEN_BRAIN_VAULT_DIR` to a temp vault since the 57-file incident in April, and `vitest.config.ts` loads it. **Root cause — CORRECTED after shipping; the first diagnosis named a real hazard but not the producer.** The demonstrated producer is **`npx vitest` run from the REPO ROOT**: there is no `vitest.config.*` above `open-brain/`, so a root-level run discovers the tests by default glob and loads **no config at all** — `setupFiles` never executes, `OPEN_BRAIN_VAULT_DIR` is never set, and the whole suite runs unisolated against the real vault. Forge's cwd had drifted to the repo root mid-session (a mirror-copy `cd`), so its full-suite runs today wrote the 13 files. Proven twice over: from the root the new guard produced **23 failures**; from `open-brain/`, 688/688 and zero new artifacts. *(Atlas's original diagnosis — `index-v2.test.ts:55`, `skill-scan-runner.test.ts:33`, `apoptosis-reachability.test.ts:138` each `delete` the variable in `afterEach` rather than restoring it, so within a reused worker every later test falls through `paths.ts` to `join(homedir(), …)` — is a **real second path to the same leak** and is also closed by the fix, but it was never shown to have produced a file. Recorded rather than deleted: two independent routes to one silent failure is the point, not a tally of who was right.)* `server.test.ts:16` is the writer in both routes — it runs session-end against `mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "ob-server-"))` and `writeSummary` deposits a summary named for the temp project. **Same invariant as the day's other four instances:** an unset `OPEN_BRAIN_VAULT_DIR` *means* "use production", so absent and configured are the same value from inside the resolver and the guard's own removal is unobservable. **Fix, two parts:** (1) `setup-env.ts` re-asserts the override in a global `afterEach`, so no teardown can leave a worker unprotected whatever it does to the variable; (2) `obsidianVaultDir()` throws when running under vitest and the path resolves to the *real* home vault — a synthetic home is still allowed, so `paths.test.ts`'s deliberate fallback assertion is untouched. Structural prevention plus a loud failure, per the v0.15.1 precedent that removing a read is not the same as counting what you no longer read. **Evidence it holds:** typecheck clean, **688 tests / 49 files green** (+1 = the new test pinning the leak), and a full suite run produced **zero** new `ob-server` files. The 13 artifacts were deleted (Aaron approved); 154 legitimate summaries remain. **What is owed next session:** confirm zero `ob-server-*` in `~/Obsidian Vault v2/Summaries/` after a fresh full run from `open-brain/`. **Revised on the /sync question** — the earlier "no check needed" was wrong, because it assumed the throw always runs, and the root-run route is precisely the case where it does not (no config, no setup, and until v0.22.1 no failure either). Two follow-ups, both filed separately: a `/sync` counter for `ob-server-*` in the vault (there is a preventer and still **no detector** — this was found by accident while listing `Summaries/` at `/end`, not by any check), and a root-level vitest config-or-refuse so a root run fails as one clear message instead of 23 scattered ones. **Also noticed, not fixed:** the artifact filenames lowercase (`ob-server-cz4uxz.md`) while the frontmatter preserves case (`ob-server-Cz4UxZ`) — invisible on Windows, two identities on Linux/macOS, the same blind spot already filed against `ob_store` deriving vault folder names from a canonicalized path. - [ ] **T-050** v0.15.1 made a foreign `.recalled-entries.json` writer unreachable *and* uncountable — (Session 50, surfaced by Prime). Prime confirmed it does not write that path, then correctly advised refusing foreign writers loudly anyway — a future harness version is not bound by today's inventory. That property cannot be built as described: v0.15.1's fix was not a `session_id` comparison but the **removal of the read** (precedence: explicit ids → `recall_log` → the file only if the session is unknown → nothing). On the normal path there is no read, so no refusal, so nothing to report. Net effect: **"no foreign writer" and "a foreign writer never looked at" are the same observation from inside the resolver.** This is a fourth instance of the dropped-count invariant above, sitting inside the fix that shipped this morning — the bad case was made unreachable and thereby uncountable. Fix: split observation from authority — a detector that reads the file purely to *report* and never to resolve ids, preserving the structural guarantee that the file cannot influence which entries get rated. Do **not** reopen v0.15.1; the correctness fix is right, this adds detection on top. General form worth carrying: **removing a read is not the same as counting what you no longer read** — structural prevention makes a failure impossible and simultaneously invisible, which is correct while the failure cannot recur and a blind spot the moment a new writer can appear.

- [ ] **T-056** `ob_store` derives the vault folder from a canonicalized path, so it lowercases the project name — (Session 49). `server.ts:537` computes `projectName = effectiveProject.split("/").pop()` from the *canonical* `project_dir`, and `canonicalizeProjectDir` lowercases the **entire string** when it starts with a drive letter — not just the drive. Result: `ob_store` writes `Experiences/self-improving-agent/` while the `store()` pipeline given an explicit project name writes `Experiences/Self-Improving-Agent/`. **Two live rows already differ** — #235 (older) and #365 (stored during this close-out). **Invisible on Windows** because the filesystem is case-insensitive, so both resolve into the one real folder, `checkVaultIndexParity` passes, and nothing dangles. On macOS or Linux this silently creates a **second project folder**, which `skill-scan` reads as a separate project and which reproduces the exact 60-duplicate divergence repaired earlier this same session. The general rule it violates: **a canonical form is for comparison, not for display** — deriving a human-facing name from a lossy identity key reuses a transformation for a purpose it was not built for. Fix: carry the display name separately (the caller already knows it) rather than reconstructing it from the key; then repoint the two existing rows. Related to the P3 cross-platform item — this is a second Windows-only blind spot. Now documented as §10 of the `path-normalization` skill.

The durable half already knows about time and the ephemeral half does not, which is why five dead channels (TCM 2026-04-24, worthit 06-04, nexcrm 06-09, a2a-hub and openlaser 07-22) announce themselves identically to the one live one. **Same dropped-count invariant as the four instances in P1** — a letter has no status field, cannot represent *answered* or *superseded*, so absence of resolution reads as currency. **Fix (deterministic-first rule #2, remove the trigger):** surface a message **only when it postdates its channel's last decision** — no timeout constant, nothing to tune, cannot drift; unparseable headers count as unresolved and are *reported*, not skipped. - [~] **T-127** Scope 4: True self-improving loop for the protocol itself — MVP built (Session 16): protocol health scoring (sync.mjs --score), shadow-recall (session-end.mjs Stage 3), experience-reference tracking (detectReferences + reference_count). Remaining: error-scan pipeline, context efficiency instrumentation, multi-model proposer, content-overlap scoring, lineage tracking. — The Meta-Harness paper (kb #178, `meta-harness-paper-research-2026`) describes an outer loop that proposes *variants* of a harness, evaluates them against metrics, logs results, and iterates. Scopes 1-3 (built in Session 15) are consistency/maintenance tooling — they check "does the documentation match the code?" but do NOT propose improvements to the protocol's effectiveness. Scope 4 is the real self-improving loop: propose changes to how kb_recall ranks results, how session-end.mjs generates summaries, how /start surfaces knowledge, how auto-feedback rates entries — then evaluate whether the change improved actual outcomes. **Prerequisites before starting:** (1) Define metrics — recall precision (% of recalled entries rated helpful), feedback distribution (helpful vs neutral vs harmful), session duration, /end completion rate, knowledge reuse frequency across sessions. (2) Instrument the pipeline — log these metrics automatically per session so the proposer has data to reason about. (3) Re-read the Meta-Harness source material — kb #178 has a high-level summary but may lack implementation detail for the propose→evaluate→log loop mechanics. The full paper (arxiv.org/abs/2603.28052) and the project page (yoonholee.com/meta-harness/) were indexed via context-mode during Session 15 but that index is session-scoped and won't persist. **Ask Aaron:** Before diving in, re-fetch the paper and video transcript (youtube.com/watch?v=61JUHDK-em8) for complete context — the stored kb entry captures findings but not the full algorithmic detail (Section 3: formal loop definition, Appendix A: qualitative proposer behavior, Appendix B: discovered harness examples). The video adds intuition about recursive self-improvement compounding. (4) Design the evaluation harness — what does a "variant" of our protocol look like? Probably a modified session-end.mjs or kb_recall query strategy, tested against historical session data. (5) Design the proposer — an agent with full filesystem access to prior variants' code, scores, and session traces (the Meta-Harness core insight: 10M tokens of diagnostic context vs 26K for compressed methods). **Key distinction from Scopes 1-3:** Scopes 1-3 ask "is the harness internally consistent?" Scope 4 asks "is the harness *good*? Can it be *better*?" This is the difference between linting and optimization. **Open questions:** Should the loop run automatically (expensive, needs guardrails) or be agent-assisted like Scope 3 (cheaper, needs human judgment)? How many sessions of metric data do we need before the proposer has enough signal? Should variants be tested on historical data (replay) or live (A/B)? (Session 15)

- [x] **T-036** [superseded] Original finding: version skew between concurrent writers over one database (session 52) — **permitted by the architecture, detected by nothing** (Atlas, Session 52, prereg §13). MCP stdio servers are per-session subprocesses sharing one SQLite file; after a rebuild, sessions reconnect at different times, so two writers can run different builds against the same tables indefinitely. Proven live: Forge's v0.18.0-build server wrote `'explicit'` defaults while Atlas's v0.19.x server rendered the new census — 2 of 3 rows in the young explicit arm are that skew's contamination. Benign for an additive column; NOT benign for a migration that changes a column's meaning. Candidate guard, deterministic-first: stamp the build/schema version on the DB (or on each written row batch), and have `openV2Database` or a /sync check flag a writer older than the schema it writes into. Bigger than the reconnect-scoping finding it emerged from. (Session 52)

- [x] **T-104** [superseded by the item above] The mailbox protocol's truncate-to-latest rule defeats its own cross-session-persistence purpose (session 50) — (Session 50, hit live when Aaron restarted Prime mid-exchange). `~/.agents/mailbox/README.md` contains two rules that were never checked against each other. The **Lifecycle** section says truncate conversation files to just the latest message once decisions are captured, history preserved in git. The **Cross-Session Persistence** section says the mailbox exists so a restarted agent boots with a last-known-state richer than automated recall, and advises writing a summary before ending a session with significant state. Truncation actively removes that summary: **the surviving message is the least self-contained one**, because it was written assuming the context of everything truncated above it. A restarted agent reading its inbox lands mid-argument with no way to know what it missed. Worked around this session by writing an explicit rehydration brief and pointing Prime at `decisions.md` — which is cumulative, never truncated, and *is* the designed answer, so the protocol holds as long as the reader knows to start there. Fix options: state in the README that a restarted agent reads `decisions.md` first and the inbox second; or add a convention that the truncated message carries a one-line "context: see decisions.md 2026-08-11" header; or exempt the newest message from truncation when it is a reply rather than a standing brief. **Same shape as the day's other findings** — two internally sensible rules, no check that they describe the same behaviour, and the seam belonged to neither section's author.
